feature_pitch_raw:
**The pattern:** Medicare runs two separate post-hospital destinations with two separate public scorecards, and this run is the first in which both are current at the same time. CMS refreshed Inpatient Rehabilitation Facility - Provider Data and Long-Term Care Hospital - Provider Data on 09/11/26, the matching national benchmark files (Inpatient Rehabilitation Facility - National Data, Long-Term Care Hospital - National Data) on 08/12/26, and the Inpatient Rehabilitation Facility - Conditions file, first collected in this run, which counts how many times people with Medicare who had certain medical conditions were treated at each facility in the last year. Together those five files let you do the thing a discharge planner does in an afternoon and a family almost never does: put a named facility next to the national number, for your condition, before you agree to go there. The long-term care cluster is the one coherent cluster this run (cohesion 0.322, 10 items); Medicare and Medicaid is again the bigger pile at 26 items across 8 sources and again not one story.

**Why it matters:** The choice between an inpatient rehabilitation facility and a long-term care hospital is usually made in a hospital hallway, by someone else, from a list. All five of these files carry state and county geography, so the comparison is buildable down to the facility a family is actually being offered. What the Conditions file adds is volume: whether the place taking your stroke or hip is one that treated many Medicare patients with that condition last year or a handful. Nothing in these records is new law and nothing here is hidden; the stake is that the comparison exists in public and is not being made on behalf of the people who have to decide in two days.

**Why pitch this now:** The quality files refreshed 09/11/26 and the national files 08/12/26, so facility-level and benchmark numbers are aligned in the same window, which is what a chart needs. - Angle: What the restrictions mean for older lawfully present immigrants and the states that have to operationalize them, based on the brief's overview of CMS guidance.
- Hook: The 2025 reconciliation law's eligibility restrictions for many lawfully present immigrants in Medicaid and CHIP become effective 10/01/26, and the implementation brief surfaced twice in this run.
- For readers: If you or a parent are a lawfully present immigrant on Medicaid, find out now what your state is doing about the 10/01/26 change.
- For the trade: Providers serving immigrant communities face a coverage cliff on a fixed date, with state implementation still uneven.
- Why it matters: Losing Medicaid without warning means losing the care that pays for home help and prescriptions.
- Also: Confirmed gap, hard effective date, and every state handles it differently.
- Pitch to: SeniorLiving.org, Modern Healthcare

**The federal caregiving council is taking nominations and family caregivers can be nominated**
*Call for Nominations: Caregiving Advisory Council Members*  
- Angle: A short service piece on the Administration for Community Living's call for nominations, aimed at family caregivers who have never considered themselves policy participants.
- Hook: The Administration for Community Living has opened nominations for Caregiving Advisory Council members and no monitored publisher has matched it.
- For readers: If you have been caring for a parent or spouse, read the call and consider nominating yourself or someone whose experience should be on the record.
- For the trade: Provider and workforce organizations get a direct route to representation on a federal advisory body.
- Why it matters: Councils shape guidance for years, and the people doing the unpaid work are usually absent from them.
- Also: Confirmed gap and newly collected; a fast turnaround item with a deadline-driven shape.
- Pitch to: Caregiving.com, Caring.com

**Home health has added workers faster than any other corner of aging care**
*BLS: Home health care services employment, August 2026 — 1,896.40 thousands of jobs (+5.0% year over year)*  
- Angle: A read of the August 2026 home health employment print for families weighing home care against a facility, and for the agencies hiring into it.
- Hook: Home health care services employment reached 1,896.40 thousands of jobs in August 2026, up 5.0% year over year, and no monitored publisher matched the series.
- For readers: If a home care agency told you last year that no aides were available, it is worth asking again.
- For the trade: A 5.0% headcount gain sets a hiring benchmark against which individual agencies can judge their own recruiting.
- Why it matters: Whether an aide can be staffed decides whether an older adult stays home or moves.
- Also: Confirmed gap; pairs naturally with the hourly earnings series for a pay-versus-headcount chart.
- Pitch to: Next Avenue, Caring.com

**Nursing homes are still hiring at less than half the pace of home health**
*BLS: Nursing care facilities employment, August 2026 — 1,590.20 thousands of jobs (+2.1% year over year)*  
- Angle: A side-by-side of the two August 2026 employment series for readers deciding where care will actually be delivered, and for skilled nursing staffing planners.
- Hook: Nursing care facilities employment stood at 1,590.20 thousands of jobs in August 2026, up 2.1% year over year, against 5.0% growth in home health.
- For readers: Ask a nursing home you are touring how its staffing has changed in the past year, and compare the answer with the national figures.
- For the trade: The gap between the two growth rates is a recruitment story operators are competing inside, not watching from outside.
- Why it matters: Staffing levels are the single thing families notice most and are hardest to verify on a tour.
- Also: Confirmed gap; both series print monthly, so the comparison can be run again next month.
- Pitch to: Provider Magazine, McKnight's Home Care

**The program that helps you spot Medicare fraud is getting a small federal top-up**
*Announcing the Intent To Award a Single-Source Supplement to the Senior Medicare Patrol (SMP) Resource Center*  
- Angle: What the $226,000 supplement, bringing the FY 2026 award to $1,226,000, buys for the Senior Medicare Patrol network, for beneficiaries who have never heard of it.
- Hook: The Administration for Community Living announced its intent to award a $226,000 supplement to the Senior Medicare Patrol Resource Center, taking the FY 2026 total to $1,226,000.
- For readers: If a Medicare statement shows a service you never received, the Senior Medicare Patrol is who you call.
- For the trade: A resource center expansion changes what state-level fraud education partners can ask for.
- Why it matters: Most beneficiaries never learn the program exists until after they have been billed for care they did not get.
- Also: Confirmed gap; a modest figure, so the piece belongs as a service explainer rather than a funding story.
- Pitch to: SeniorLiving.org, Bankrate Retirement

**Patients graded their doctors' practices and the scores are posted**
*CMS refreshed dataset: PY 2024 Group Public Reporting: Patient Experience*  
- Angle: A guide to the CAHPS for MIPS group-level patient experience results for older adults choosing a new primary care practice.
- Hook: The PY 2024 group public reporting file carries Consumer Assessment of Healthcare Providers and Systems measures submitted by groups, refreshed 08/18/26.
- For readers: Before switching practices, check whether the group reported patient experience results and what patients said about access and communication.
- For the trade: Group-level experience scores are a recruitment and referral asset that most practices do not market.
- Why it matters: Communication and access are what older patients complain about most and what these measures actually capture.
- Also: A refreshed reference file, so the story is the how-to rather than the posting.
- Pitch to: Family Caregiver Alliance, Bankrate Retirement
